co_taylor_canyon.blurb: Taylor Canyon follows the Taylor River north of Gunnison, Colorado, and is a favorite with climbers from Crested Butte. The rock is high-quality granite in most places. Bouldering is the largest share, trad is close behind, and sport is a smaller part. Boulder problems run from V0 to V12, mostly V0 to V5, while roped climbs run from about 5.6 to 5.13, concentrated around 5.10 and 5.11. Most routes are one or two pitches, some are runout, and the grades can feel stiff. First Buttress is the busiest wall: it tilts slightly north, the left side is sunny all day and the right side gets shade late in the afternoon, so it suits the warmer months. Graveyard Boulders and Second Buttress are other larger zones.

co_upper_dream_canyon.blurb: Upper Dream Canyon is a secluded canyon near Boulder, Colorado, at roughly 7,500 feet, with a gentle feel. Bolts protect most of the climbing: sport leads the way, a solid trad group follows, and there are about a dozen boulder problems and a couple of top-ropes. The grades lean hard, running from about 5.8 to the low 5.13s with the heaviest weight between 5.10 and 5.12. Lost Angel, described as the largest piece of granite in the Boulder area, holds the most climbs, with routes of one to five pitches. Midnight Rock, Dream Dome and Oceanic Wall come next. Some route starts get tricky during spring runoff.

md_cunningham_falls_state_park.blurb: Cunningham Falls State Park sits in the Catoctin Mountains of Frederick County, Maryland, and its climbing is modest in scale. Top-rope climbs and bouldering share most of it, with only a handful of trad leads. Boulder problems run from V0 to V7, and roped climbs mostly fall between 5.6 and 5.10 with little harder. Cliff Trail Boulders is the largest bouldering cluster, holding most of the better problems, while Cat Rock and Big Big Roof offer a mix of trad and top-rope. Cat Rock's summit is light gray quartzite, metamorphosed sandstone, with ragged outcrops and large boulders piled beneath. More outcrops and boulders lie deeper in the woods.

nh_wm_pinkham_presidentials.blurb: Pinkham / Presidentials covers Pinkham Notch and the high Presidential Range in New Hampshire's White Mountains, with crags on both sides of the notch and big mountain terrain above. Trad leads the mix, with a sizable bouldering contingent, a good amount of winter ice, some alpine and mountaineering routes, and a little sport. Rock routes run from about 5.4 to 5.12, clustered around 5.7 and 5.8, while ice runs from WI1 to WI5. Hall's Ledge and Mount Washington are the biggest sub-areas, followed by Square Ledge and the Gorham slabs. Huntington Ravine holds long multi-pitch trad on rough schist, and weather up there can turn severe quickly; summits can be far colder than the valleys.

va_1_mile_one.blurb: Mile One is the first of the climbing zones in Guest River Gorge, near Coeburn in Southwest Virginia, where the zones are numbered by the trail's mile markers. It leans toward bouldering, with a solid number of bolted routes and only a little trad. Boulder problems run from V0 to V9, mostly V1 to V8, and roped climbs run from about 5.6 to the low 5.13s, mostly between 5.9 and 5.11. It is the second-largest zone in the gorge, after Mile Two, and splits into a boulder section and a routes section. Routes across the gorge are mostly sport.

nm_ponderosa_bouldering.blurb: Ponderosa Bouldering sits in the Jemez Mountains of northern New Mexico and is almost entirely boulder problems on volcanic tuff. Where the surface is thin the rock is grainy and gives pocketed faces; it is sharp and coarse, so it is hard on skin. The terrain ranges from thin faces and slabs to steep overhanging blocks, with both low and high boulders, and problems run from V0 to V12, mostly V2 to V6. The Pond is the biggest zone, followed by Big Cat Canyon and The Satellite. The setting is arid, dusty and very exposed to sun, and after snowmelt the lower slopes at the Pond turn muddy, so higher sandier ground is better then.
